articles.summary: HR Spotlight HR Spotlight: Elizabeth Odetokun on Taking Charge of Your Career Oluwakemi Adesina November 14, 2026 Elizabeth Odetokun once had to fight for a seat at a meeting she knew she belonged in. She was the HR Manager at Mainstack. The company’s leaders made decisions without her but when problems surfaced, they expected her to solve them. So she went to the founders and asked why HR wasn’t part of those conversations. It takes courage to fight for something you believe you should already have. She eventually got her seat at the table but she made it clear that the experience wasn’t pleasant. Staying quiet would cost her the opportunity to learn and do more. She would also miss the chance to work closely with the company’s leaders. For her, that was too much to give up. “Your number one responsibility is your career,” she said during the interview. That belief has shaped how Elizabeth handles work. Six years ago, Elizabeth was an HR intern learning payroll through Google. Today, she works with founders on HR, strategy and business operations. None of it would have happened if she waited for someone to recognise her potential. How do you build a career in something you never planned for? Elizabeth initially wanted to study Economics at Obafemi Awolowo University. She wanted to attend the school so badly that she still laughs about it today. “For the life of me, I can’t even remember why I wanted to go to that school.” she said. She didn’t pass the post-UTME but got into Lagos State University and chose not to attend. The school was far from home, and she had concerns about safety. Then a family friend suggested the University of Lagos. He also advised her to consider Human Resources, a course she knew almost nothing about. His selling point was simple; with HR, she could work in almost any industry. That sounded good enough to Elizabeth, so she went on to study HR at the University of Lagos. But it took her first internship in 2019 to find out what working in HR really meant. On her first day, she had to screen 30 to 40 job applicants, with no prior experience. Soon, she was managing over 100 workers at the APM Terminal in Apapa. She handled recruitment, medical checks, onboarding and payroll. Remember, this was an intern who just left school. “I didn’t feel like an intern at all,” she recalled. She had never prepared payroll before, let alone for 100 people. There was no detailed training to fall back on. So she turned to Google to learn how to draft memos, prepare payroll and complete other tasks. She often worked late because she was afraid of making mistakes. The working conditions weren’t great either. The company even cut her pay when she refused to work on some weekends. She could have left, other interns did but Elizabeth had made a deal with herself. She would spend six months there, give the job her best and leave with experience she needed. That experience taught Elizabeth a lesson she still lives by. She couldn’t control everything at work, but she could choose how to respond. As her career grew, she took that lesson with her. It helped her take on bigger roles, even when she lacked all the answers. What happens when your role outgrows your experience? At Bundle Africa, Elizabeth started out handling recruitment, employee engagement and performance reviews. Then the company restructured, and her senior manager left. Elizabeth began reporting directly to the Chief Operating Officer. Suddenly, her responsibilities went far beyond managing people. She had to review departmental budgets, check invoices and question spending. She also checked how the customer service team spoke to customers. If something wasn’t right, she asked them to fix it. It was unfamiliar work, but she didn’t shy away from it. She recalls asking department heads to explain expenses worth thousands of dollars. “What’s going on here? What are we hoping to get here?” She laughed as she told me how much she enjoyed having the authority to ask those questions. “I had power, so I enjoyed having that power.” But with that authority came more responsibility. She had to understand the numbers, pay attention to details and defend her decisions. She couldn’t approve something simply because a department head had submitted it. The finance team began to notice her work. One colleague was so impressed by her attention to detail that they asked if she had done the work before. She hadn’t. She was learning every day and she wanted to do the work well. That period changed how Elizabeth saw her place in a business. She began to see how each part of the business worked and how the decisions made in one team affected the others. She also realised that she could contribute to conversations beyond HR. What if nobody makes room for you at the table? When Elizabeth joined Mainstack, she brought that confidence with her. But she faced a new problem. She wasn’t present in leadership meetings. She had worked across different areas of business operations. She understood why HR needed to know what was happening across the company. Yet she still had to make her case. Companies often involve HR in hiring and staff matters. But HR rarely gets a seat at the table when leaders make business decisions. Elizabeth admits that some HR professionals also stick to these duties, but she wanted to do more. She had shown this curiosity before. At Sygnite, a renewable energy company, she wanted to understand more than HR. She learnt about suppliers, equipment costs, profit margins and what the engineers did. She wasn’t trying to become an engineer. She wanted to understand what they do so she could make better decisions about the people on those teams. At Mainstack, she put that curiosity to work by pushing for a place in leadership meetings. It wasn’t easy, and she didn’t enjoy
articles.title: HR Spotlight: Elizabeth Odetokun on Taking Charge of Your Career
